summary: This unit teaches you to plan and apply nail art safely and neatly: consult with the client, check her nails for contraindications, plan a balanced design with the colour wheel, and prepare the natural nails. You will learn freehand and tool techniques (dots, stripes, sponged ombre, French tips, marbling and stamping), add gems, decals and foils, work with gel polish, and finish, remove, advise and record to a professional standard.

blocks.p: This unit covers the whole nail art service, from the moment you greet the client to the moment you clean your brushes and fill in her record card. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and it builds on the manicure skills of preparing, shaping and polishing natural nails.

Good nail art is neat, balanced and suits the client, her occasion and her daily life, and it lasts. Careless nail art chips in a day, spreads infection from nail to nail, gives the client an allergy to gel, or starts a fire from the solvents on the station. So this unit is about **safety, hygiene and planning** as much as painting skill.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two practical tasks. In one, your group makes a themed display board of practice tips using at least five different techniques. In the other, you give nail art to a client's natural nails for an occasion, with an accent nail on each hand. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, hygiene, method, finish and records, not only the finished nails.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hands, the nails, the tips and the work area. Never photograph a client's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Nail art products give off fumes, most of them burn easily, and some can cause allergies. Germs travel from client to client on dirty tools, files and towels. Learn these habits before you pick up a brush.

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Fumes from polish, remover, gel cleanser and adhesives
Headache, dizziness, sore eyes and throat; breathing problems over time
Work with fresh air: open windows, or use a fan or extraction that draws fumes away from both your faces
Keep lids on bottles except while you load the brush
Use small amounts; keep remover in a pump dispenser
Flammable products (remover, polish, top coat, gel cleanser)
Fire
Keep them away from heat, sparks and flames: candles, cigarettes, wax heaters, hot tools
No smoking near the station
Put solvent-soaked cotton in a lidded metal bin
Uncured gel, nail glue and other products on the skin
Allergy (red, itchy, swollen skin); glue can bond skin together
Keep products off the skin and cuticles
Clean off any spill before you cure gel
Wear gloves when handling these products
Dust from filing
Irritated nose, throat and eyes
Wear a dust mask when filing gel or making a lot of dust
Use extraction if the station has it; brush dust away, do not blow it
Splashes into the eyes
Stinging; injury to the eye
Pump dispensers; lids on
Keep products below the client's face level
Know where the eye wash is
Sharp tools and rough gems
Cuts, which let germs in
Handle nippers and scissors with care
Check that no gem, charm or broken decal has a sharp edge
Poor light, a wobbly table, a bad chair
Messy work; eye strain; neck and back pain
Bright light on the nails, a stable table and a hand rest
Chair at a height that keeps your back straight; take short breaks
LED or UV lamp and its cable
Electric shock; trips
Check the cable and plug before use
Keep liquids away from the lamp; dry your hands
Keep cables off the floor and walkways

blocks.note: Jamaica is hot, and solvents give off more vapour in the heat. A closed, air-conditioned room traps fumes, so use extraction or let fresh air in, and keep every bottle closed between strokes. The power supply is 110 V at 50 Hz: check that a lamp is made for the socket you plug it into.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Keep every product in its own **labelled** container with the lid closed tightly. Never pour remover into a drinks bottle or an unlabelled bottle.
Store products in a cool, dark place, away from direct sun, heat and flames, away from food and drink, and out of reach of children.
Keep only what you need at the station. Use the oldest stock first and check expiry dates.
If polish has gone thick, use a polish thinner if the maker allows it, or throw the polish away. **Never thin polish with remover**: it spoils the polish.

Put cotton, pads and wipes soaked in remover or gel cleanser in a **lidded metal bin**, and empty it often (at least every day) into the outside bin. The lid keeps the fumes in and stops a fire spreading.
Other waste (used files, orange sticks, wipes without solvent) goes in a lined, lidded bin.
Read the **safety data sheet** (SDS) for each chemical product. It tells you its hazards, safe use, storage, what to do with a spill and the first aid.

blocks.h: First aid at the nail station

head: Accident
What you do
rows: Product splashes into an eye
Rinse the eye at once with plenty of clean, cool running water or sterile eye wash, for at least 10 minutes, holding the eyelids open
Tilt the head so the water runs away from the other eye; do not let her rub it
Get medical help if it still hurts or looks red; record it
Product on the skin
Wash it off with soap and water
Nail glue on the skin: soak in warm, soapy water and ease the skin apart gently; never pull it
Dizziness or headache from fumes
Stop work; take her into fresh air and let her sit
Close the bottles and ventilate the room
Get medical help if she does not feel better
A small cut from nippers
Stop; put on gloves
Press with clean cotton until it stops; cover it
Bin the cotton in a lined bin; do not work on that finger
A burning feeling under the lamp (heat spike)
Take the hand out of the lamp at once
Let it cool, then finish the cure; apply thinner layers next time
A product is swallowed
Do not make her vomit
Get medical help at once and take the label or SDS with you

head: Item
What you do
rows: Hands
You wash your hands before and after each client. The client washes hers, or you clean them with an antibacterial product.
Station
Wipe the table, hand rest and lamp with salon disinfectant; lay a fresh towel for each client.
Single-use items
Orange sticks, cotton, lint-free wipes, ombre sponges, disposable spatulas, and paper or foam files and buffers are used on one client only, then go in a lined, lidded bin.
Metal tools (dotting tools, pushers, nippers, tweezers, scissors)
Remove product and dust, wash with soap and water, rinse and dry, then disinfect for the full contact time on the label (or sterilise). Store them in a clean, covered container.
Glass and metal files
Wash and disinfect them as the maker says; otherwise treat files as single-use.
Nail art brushes
Wipe and clean straight after use with the right cleaner (see below), reshape the bristles and store them covered.
Stamping plates and stampers
Clean off the polish straight after use, as the maker says.
Towels
A fresh towel for every client; used towels go straight into a closed laundry bin.

blocks.note: A UV cabinet only keeps clean, disinfected tools clean while they are stored. It does **not** disinfect dirty tools. Disinfectant cannot work through polish or dust, so always clean first, then disinfect.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Product on the brush
Clean it with
Take care
rows: Water-based nail art paint
Clean water, while the paint is still wet; then wipe on a lint-free wipe
Do not let paint dry in the bristles; harsh solvents spoil the brush.
Ordinary polish
Polish remover, then wipe on a lint-free wipe
Reshape the bristles to a point or a flat edge.
Gel polish or gel paint
Wipe the brush on a lint-free wipe, then the gel cleanser the maker gives
Store gel brushes capped, away from daylight and the lamp: light cures gel left in the bristles and the brush goes hard.
Foil adhesive or water-based glue
Water (or as the maker says), straight away
Glue left to dry ruins the brush.

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters in nail art
rows: Nail plate
The hard, see-through layers of keratin (a protein) that you paint on.
Oil and dust on it stop polish sticking. Over-filing and peeling gel make it thin and weak.
Free edge
The part of the nail that grows past the end of the finger.
You cap it with base coat, colour and top coat to seal it. Its length decides how much design fits.
Nail bed
The skin under the nail plate. It looks pink because of the blood vessels in it.
If the plate lifts away from the bed, germs and product can get underneath.
Matrix
Hidden under the skin at the base of the nail. It makes the new nail cells.
An injury here can cause dents, ridges or white marks that grow out with the nail. Never dig at the base of the nail.
Lunula
The pale half-moon at the base of the nail: the part of the matrix you can see.
Half-moon designs follow its curve.
Cuticle
A thin layer of dead skin stuck to the nail plate at the base.
Push it back and remove only the loose dead skin; polish on it lifts and chips.
Eponychium
The living fold of skin at the base of the nail (people often call it the cuticle too).
Never cut it: it seals out germs.
Hyponychium
The skin under the free edge.
It also seals out germs; do not dig under the free edge.
Side walls and grooves
The skin at each side of the nail plate.
Keep polish off them; leave a hairline gap.

blocks.note: Fingernails grow about 3 mm a month, so a whole nail takes about 4 to 6 months to grow out. Damage from peeling gel or a knock to the matrix stays visible for months.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Shape
What it looks like
Suits
rows: Square
A straight free edge with sharp, square corners.
Strong nails; long, narrow nail beds. The corners can catch and break.
Squoval (square oval)
A straight free edge with softly rounded corners.
Most clients; strong and practical for busy hands.
Round
Follows the curve of the fingertip, with little length.
Short nails, men, and clients with active jobs.
Oval
Rounded sides and tip, like an egg.
Medium-length nails; makes fingers look slimmer.
Almond
The sides taper to a soft, rounded point.
Slim fingers and strong nails with some length; weaker at the tip than a square or squoval.

blocks.note: Very long, pointed (stiletto) and coffin shapes usually need nail extensions, which are taught in another unit.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Greet the client and read her record card
Ask your questions
Look at her hands and nails in good light
Check for contraindications
Show your portfolio and sample tips
Agree the design, products, time and price
Record it; the client signs

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: The occasion and the date; her outfit, colours and theme
The design must suit the event and last as long as she needs it (polish lasts a few days; gel lasts about 2 to 3 weeks).
Her job, hobbies and daily life
Some jobs (health care, food handling, child care) have rules about nail length and decoration. Typing, cleaning and hands in water wear art down, and gems and 3D charms can snag.
Allergies and past reactions (gel, nail glue, polish, latex)
You can choose a different product. An allergy to gel is usually for life.
Health problems and medicines that affect the skin or nails
Some need extra care or a doctor's advice first.
Her home habits: how she removes polish; whether she peels gel
Shapes your aftercare advice.
Her budget and the time she has
So the design fits the booking and the agreed price.

blocks.note: Clients find it hard to describe nail art in words. Show them your portfolio, practice tips and a colour chart, and sketch the design before you start. Agree every detail, including which nails are accent nails.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is something that stops the service, or means you must change it. An infection or infestation that can spread **stops** work on that nail and needs a referral. Other conditions **restrict** the service: you adapt it, or leave a nail out.

head: Condition
What you see
Can it spread?
What you do
rows: Fungal infection of the nail (onychomycosis)
A thick, yellow, brown or white nail that may crumble or lift.
Yes
Do not work on the nail. Refer her to a doctor or pharmacist.
Bacterial infection around the nail (paronychia)
Red, swollen, hot, painful skin around the nail; sometimes pus.
Yes
Do not work on the nail. Refer her to a doctor.
Green or green-black patch under a lifted nail or old gel
A bacterial infection trapped under the plate or product.
Yes
Do not cover it. Refer her to a doctor.
Warts around the nail
Rough, raised lumps (caused by a virus).
Yes
Do not work over them. Refer her.
Cuts, broken, bleeding or weeping skin
Open skin.
No, but germs get in
Avoid the area; postpone if it is large. Products sting and germs can enter.
Nail lifting from the nail bed (onycholysis)
A white or cloudy area under the free edge where the plate has come away.
No (unless infected)
Restrict: keep it short, use a light design, and never push tools or product under the plate. Suggest a doctor if it does not improve or changes colour.
Bruised nail
A dark red, purple or black patch under the plate after a knock.
No
Restrict: work gently with no pressure; refer if it is painful.
Split, peeling or very weak nails
Layers coming apart at the free edge; soft, bendy nails.
No
Restrict: gentle preparation, short length, a light design.
White spots (leuconychia)
Small white flecks, usually from small knocks.
No
Carry on: they are not a contraindication.
Ridges
Lines running from the base to the tip; common with age.
No
Carry on; a ridge-filling base coat smooths them. Buff only lightly.
Bitten nails
Short nails with ragged edges.
No
Carry on with small, simple designs; avoid any broken skin.
Allergy to a nail product
Itchy, red, swollen skin around the nails, or on the face and eyelids, after a past service.
No
Do not use that product; offer another (for example, ordinary polish instead of gel). Refer her if the skin is reacting now.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not name a disease. Tell the client quietly and kindly what you have seen, explain why you cannot work on that nail today, and advise her to see a doctor or pharmacist. Many salons postpone the whole service when a nail is infected, because tools and hands can carry it to her other nails: follow the Centre's rules. Record what you found.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: After a client with an infection: throw away every single-use item you used, clean and then disinfect your tools and the station, and wash your hands.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Planning the design: colour and balance

blocks.p: Plan the design before you open a bottle. A design that looks good on paper may be far too busy on a short nail, and a client who agreed to 'something pretty' may not like what you paint. A plan agreed with the client avoids both problems.

head: Group
Colours
What to know
rows: Primary
Red, yellow, blue
They cannot be mixed from other colours.
Secondary
Orange (red + yellow), green (yellow + blue), purple (blue + red)
Each is an equal mix of two primaries.
Tertiary
Red-orange, yellow-green, blue-purple and so on
A primary mixed with the secondary next to it.
Neutrals and metallics
Black, white, grey, nude, gold, silver
They frame bright colours and calm a design; gold and silver lines and foils add highlights.

ul: A **tint** is a colour with white added (lighter); a **shade** is a colour with black added (darker); a **tone** has grey added (softer). Mix nail art paints on a palette to make them.
**Warm** colours (reds, oranges, yellows) look lively and bright. **Cool** colours (blues, greens, purples) look calm and fresh.

head: Scheme
What it is
The effect
Example
rows: Complementary
Two colours opposite each other on the wheel
The strongest contrast: bold, and it shows up from a distance. Use one as the main colour and the other as the accent.
Red and green; blue and orange; yellow and purple
Analogous (harmonious)
Colours next to each other on the wheel
Calm and blended; ideal for an ombre.
Blue, blue-green and green
Monochromatic
Tints and shades of one colour
Simple and elegant; suits work and formal wear.
Pale pink, rose and deep rose
Triadic
Three colours evenly spaced on the wheel
Lively and playful.
Red, yellow and blue

head: Principle
What it means on nails
rows: Balance
Both hands look like a matching pair. Put the accent nail on the same finger of each hand (often the ring finger) and repeat the same colours on both.
Focal point
One place the eye goes to first: usually the **accent nail**, which carries the most detail. Keep the other nails simpler so they support it.
Proportion
The size of the design suits the size of the nail: small motifs on short nails; more room for scenes on long ones.
Repetition
Repeating a colour, a line or a shape across the nails ties the design together.
Contrast
Light on dark (or dark on light) shows up clearly; colours close together look soft.
Line
**Vertical** lines make nails look longer and slimmer; **horizontal** bands make them look shorter and wider. Pale colours make a nail look bigger; very dark ones make it look smaller.

blocks.note: Less is more. On short nails, one well-placed motif or a fine line looks better than ten busy nails. Keep 3D charms and large gems for long nails and accent nails.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Matching the design to the client

head: Client or occasion
Ideas that suit
rows: Short nails or an active job
Dots, fine stripes, small flat decals, one accent nail per hand; no 3D charms.
Long, strong nails
Ombre, marbling, freehand scenes, gems on the accent nails.
Work, church or a quiet style
Nude, pale or monochromatic colours; a fine gold stripe; a neat French tip; small flowers.
Weddings
White, nude and pastels, French tips, small pearls or gems; match the wedding colours.
Festivals and national days
Bold colours and strong contrast; a national or school theme.
Beach and sun
Bright tropical colours, flowers and leaves; gel lasts better in sea and sun.

blocks.note: Jamaica's national symbols make good themes: the flag's **black, green and gold** (black for the strength and creativity of the people, gold for the sunlight and natural wealth, green for hope and the land), the blue flowers of the lignum vitae (the national flower), and the green doctor bird with its long black tail feathers.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Work out how long each technique will take. Detailed hand-painting on ten nails takes far longer than dots or stripes.
Check that the design fits the time booked; if it does not, suggest a simpler design or book a longer appointment.
Tell the client the **full price in J$ before you start**, including extras such as gems or gel. If she asks for more art part-way through, agree the new price first.
Sketch the plan on a design sheet or paint it on a practice tip, and write it on the record card.

head: Tool
What it does
Tip
rows: Striper brush
Long, thin bristles that hold enough paint for a long, fine, straight line in one stroke.
Load the whole length of the bristles; do not press down.
Detail (liner) brush
Short, fine bristles for small shapes, outlines and flower centres.
Use a little paint at a time.
Flat (shader) brush
French tips, petals, smile lines and blocks of colour.
Can be loaded with two colours for one-stroke petals.
Angled brush
Clean-up around the cuticle; crisp smile lines.
Keep one just for clean-up with remover.
Fan brush
Soft streaks and feathered effects; blending; flicking on glitter.
Use it almost dry, with a light touch.
Dotting tool
A small metal ball on a handle; makes neat round dots. Different ball sizes make different dots.
Re-dip for every dot, or every two, so the dots stay the same size.
Small sponge
Dabs on colours for an ombre (gradient).
Single-use.
Striping tape
Thin adhesive tape for straight lines: as a guide, or left on as a stripe.
Press the edges down firmly.
Stamping plate, scraper and stamper
A metal plate with etched designs, a scraper to remove extra polish, and a soft stamper to pick up the design and press it on the nail.
Work quickly; clean them straight after use.
Wax pencil (gem picker)
Picks up and places gems.
A slightly damp dotting tool also works.
Fine tweezers
Place decals, foils and charms.
Clean and disinfect after use.
Toothpick or marbling needle
Drags colours to make swirls in marbling.
Wipe it after each drag.
Palette
Holds a small amount of paint for dipping and mixing.
Do not dip tools straight into the pot.
Orange stick
Pushing back cuticles, cleaning up, pressing gems and foil.
Single-use.

head: Product
What it does
Key points
rows: Nail cleanser (dehydrator)
Removes oil, dust and moisture from the nail plate so products stick.
Use after shaping, before the base coat; do not touch the plates afterwards.
Base coat
Protects the nail, stops strong colours staining it, and helps the colour grip.
One thin coat; cap the free edge. A ridge-filling base smooths ridges.
Nail polish
The colour.
Thin coats; roll the bottle, do not shake it.
Nail art paint
Bright, water-based paint for detail; dries fast.
Clean the brush with water; always seal it with top coat.
Stamping polish
Thick, strongly coloured polish, so a thin printed line still shows.
Ordinary polish is often too thin to stamp well.
Top coat
Seals and protects the design and adds shine (or a matt finish).
Cover every bit of art; cap the free edge.
Quick-dry drops or spray
Help the surface of wet polish dry faster.
The polish underneath stays soft for some time.
Gel polish (base, colour, top coat)
Stays soft until cured under an LED or UV lamp; lasts about 2 to 3 weeks.
Thin layers; cure each as the maker says; soak-off removal.
Gel paint and gel liner
Thick gel for detail that does not move until cured.
Cure each layer of art.
Foil adhesive (foil glue)
Holds transfer foil.
Goes on milky white, turns clear and tacky when ready.
Nail glue or gem gel
Holds gems and charms.
Keep it off the skin.
Polish remover
Acetone remover works fast and is needed to soak off gel, but it is very drying. Non-acetone remover is gentler and slower.
Both are flammable.
Gel cleanser
Wipes the sticky layer off cured gel; cleans gel brushes.
Use the one the gel maker gives.
Cuticle oil
Softens the cuticles and keeps the nails flexible.
For finishing and for home care.

ul: A stable table at a comfortable height, with a hand rest or cushion for the client.
Bright light (a daylight lamp is best) shining on the nails, not into anyone's eyes.
Your chair set so your back is straight and your feet are flat; the client seated comfortably facing you.
Products and tools laid out in the order you will use them, on a fresh towel.
A lined, lidded bin and a lidded metal bin within reach; remover in a pump dispenser.
Fresh air or extraction working; the lamp placed safely with its cable tidy.
Your portfolio, sample tips, colour chart, price list in J$ and the record card ready.

blocks.note: Steady your painting hand by resting your little finger on the table or on the client's hand. Hold her finger gently and roll it slightly to reach the side walls, and turn her hand rather than twisting your own body.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Preparing the nails and applying colour

blocks.p: Nail art lasts only as long as the base under it. Oil, dust or a missed free edge will make the best design chip or peel within a day or two.

flow: Wash your hands; the client washes or sanitises hers
Remove old polish
Check the nails and skin again for contraindications
Shape the nails
Push back the cuticles and remove only loose dead skin
Buff lightly if needed and brush away the dust
Wipe each nail with nail cleanser
Apply a thin base coat, capping the free edge
Apply two thin colour coats, capping each
Let it dry (or cure gel) before the art

ul: **Removing old polish:** hold a pad soaked in remover on the nail for a few seconds so it dissolves the polish, then wipe from the base to the tip in one stroke. Less rubbing means less staining of the skin. Clean the side walls with cotton on an orange stick.

**Shaping:** use a fine file (180 to 240 grit is usual for natural nails). File from each side towards the centre in one direction. Sawing back and forth splits and frays the layers of the nail. Do not file deep into the corners, which weakens the nail.
**Cuticles:** soften them, then push them back gently with a pusher or an orange stick. Remove only loose dead skin; never cut the living skin, and never dig at the base, where the matrix is.
**Buffing:** a light buff removes shine so gel can grip. Do not over-buff: it thins the nail plate.
**Cleansing:** wipe each nail with nail cleanser on a lint-free wipe to remove oil, dust and moisture. From now on, do not touch the nail plates: the oil from your fingers stops products sticking.
**Base coat:** one thin coat over the whole nail, capping the free edge, kept off the skin.

flow: Wipe one side of the brush on the neck of the bottle
Place the brush in the centre of the nail, just short of the cuticle
Push gently towards the cuticle so the bristles fan out
Pull the brush down to the tip
Paint one stroke down each side
Run the brush along the free edge to cap it
Leave a hairline gap at the cuticle and side walls

ul: Two thin coats are better than one thick coat. Thick coats stay soft underneath, wrinkle, bubble and smudge.
Let each coat become touch dry before the next. Ordinary polish can stay soft underneath for hours, even when the top feels dry.
In hot weather, open polish thickens fast: close each bottle as soon as you have loaded the brush.

head: Problem
Likely cause
Prevention or cure
rows: Air bubbles
Shaking the bottle; thick coats; old, thick polish; damp nails
Roll the bottle between your palms; thin coats; dry nails; let each coat dry.
Streaks
Too little polish; overworking it
Load enough polish; three strokes; a second coat.
Polish flooding the cuticle or side walls
Too much on the brush; brush too close to the skin
Clean up at once with a fine brush dipped in remover; leave a hairline gap.
Chips at the tip
Free edge not capped; oil on the plate; no base coat
Cleanse the plate; cap every layer.
Peeling off in sheets
Oil or moisture on the plate; no base coat
Cleanse with nail cleanser; always use a base coat.
Smudges and dents
Touched before it was dry
Wait; use quick-dry; ask the client to pay and find her keys before the top coat.
Wrinkled surface
Coats too thick
Thin coats, each left to dry.
Yellow stains on the nail
Strong colours put on with no base coat
Always use a base coat.

blocks.p: Practise each technique on practice tips until it is neat before you use it on a client. Work in thin layers, let each layer dry, and seal everything with top coat at the end.

head: Technique
How to do it
Get it right
rows: Dotting
Dip the ball of the dotting tool into paint on the palette, touch the nail lightly and lift straight up.
Bigger ball, bigger dot
Re-dip every dot or two for even dots; without re-dipping, the dots get smaller (useful for a fade)
Five dots in a ring make a flower; two dots dragged together make a heart
Freehand stripes
Load a striper brush along its whole length, rest your hand, and pull one smooth stroke from one end to the other without pressing.
Turn the finger, not the brush, for curves
Paint that is too thick drags; thin it slightly
Striping tape as a guide
On a completely dry base colour, press the tape down firmly, paint over it, then peel the tape off while the top colour is still slightly wet.
Pull the tape back over itself, slowly and evenly
Seal with top coat when dry
Striping tape as a stripe
Press the tape onto the dry colour, trim it just short of the free edge and the skin, and seal it.
Ends left loose will lift and catch.
Sponged ombre (gradient)
Over a pale base, paint two or three colours side by side on a sponge and dab them onto the nail with light pressure; repeat two or three times to build colour.
Protect the skin with tape or a peel-off barrier
Clean up the skin; top coat smooths the tiny bubbles and blends the colours
French tip
On a pink or nude base, paint the tip white (or a colour) with a flat or angled brush, or use guide stickers.
The smile line follows the natural curve of the free edge
Every nail has the same depth and curve, on both hands
Half-moon (reverse French)
Paint the base of the nail to follow the curve of the lunula, leaving it bare or in a contrast colour.
Clean, even curves on every nail.
Fan brush effects
Load an almost dry fan brush with a little paint and flick it lightly across the nail for streaks or feathers.
Build up slowly; it is easy to overload.
Water marbling

Drop polishes one at a time into a cup of room-temperature water to form rings; drag a toothpick through them to make a pattern; dip the nail in at an angle; clean the water's surface with an orange stick before you lift the finger out.
Protect the skin first with tape or a peel-off barrier
Use fresh polish and work quickly
Clean up, then top coat
Dry marbling
Drop small dots of colour onto wet polish and swirl them with a needle or fine dotting tool.
Wipe the needle after each swirl.
Stamping

Paint stamping polish over a design on the plate; scrape off the extra in one quick, firm stroke (scraper at about 45°); at once roll the stamper over the design to pick it up; roll it onto the nail from one side to the other.
Speed matters: the polish dries on the plate in seconds
Clean the plate and stamper straight away
Let the print dry; float the top coat on without dragging
Freehand painting
Paint simple shapes (petals, leaves, hibiscus flowers, palm leaves) with a detail or flat brush; build from big shapes to small details; outline last.
Keep the brush fairly upright and the strokes short.
One-stroke painting
Load a flat brush with two colours, one on each corner; one stroke makes a shaded petal or leaf.
Practise on tips first.

blocks.note: Nail art paint is water-based and wears off if it is not sealed. Every design, and every gem, decal and foil, finishes under a top coat that also caps the free edge.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Faults and how to fix them

head: Fault
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Stamped image has gaps or missing pieces
Too slow between scraping and picking up, so the polish dried on the plate; polish too thin; dirty or worn plate
Work quickly; use stamping polish; clean the plate; press the stamper on firmly enough.
Stamped image smears
Top coat brushed across it, or the print was still wet
Let it dry; float a thick bead of top coat on without pressing.
Ragged edges on taped lines
Tape peeled after the polish had set; tape edges not pressed down; base still soft
Peel while slightly wet; press the edges; let the base dry first.
Dots of different sizes
Not re-dipping; paint too thick or too thin; pressing too hard
Re-dip; adjust the paint; touch and lift.
Wobbly lines
Brush overloaded; hand not supported; stopping part-way
Rest your hand; one smooth stroke; less paint.
Colours drag and mix
Painting over a layer that is still wet
Let each layer dry.
Marbling rings do not spread
Water too cold or too hot; old or quick-dry polish; working too slowly
Room-temperature water; fresh polish; work quickly.

blocks.note: For a themed board or a client's ten nails, plan which technique goes on which nail. Mixing two or three techniques that share the same colours looks planned; using every technique at once looks messy.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Gems, decals, foils and gel nail art

flow: Let the colour dry (or cure the gel)
Put a small dot of top coat, gel or nail glue where the gem will sit
Pick the gem up with a wax pencil or a slightly damp dotting tool
Place it and press it gently so it sits flat
Seal around its edges with top coat (or gel, then cure)
Check that nothing is loose or sharp

ul: Seal around the base of a faceted crystal rather than over its top: top coat over the facets dulls the sparkle.
Keep gems away from the free edge and the cuticle, where they catch and lift.
Use small, flat gems on short nails and on clients who use their hands a lot. Keep larger stones and 3D charms for accent nails on longer nails.
Gel or nail glue holds bigger stones better than top coat alone.

head: Type
How to apply it
rows: Sticker decal (self-adhesive)
Apply on dry polish
Lift it with tweezers and place it
Press it flat from the centre outwards to push out air
Trim any overhang; seal with top coat, capping the free edge
Water-slide decal
Cut it out and soak it in water for a few seconds, until it slides on its backing
Slide it onto the nail and smooth it with a damp orange stick
Blot the water with a lint-free wipe and let it dry
Seal with top coat

flow: Let the base colour dry
Brush a thin layer of foil adhesive where the foil should go
Wait until it changes from milky white to clear and tacky
Lay the foil on with the shiny (coloured) side facing up
Press and rub it firmly with an orange stick or your finger
Peel it off quickly in one movement
Repeat on any gaps, then seal

blocks.note: Some top coats wrinkle foil. Test your top coat on a practice tip first; a gel top coat often seals foil well.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Gel polish stays soft until it is **cured** (hardened) under an LED or UV lamp. That gives you time to work, but it also means any gel left on the skin stays soft and can cause an allergy.

head: Step
What you do
Why
rows: Prepare
Prepare the nails as usual, buff off the shine lightly, then cleanse (and prime, if the maker says).
Gel grips a clean, matt plate.
Gel base coat
One thin coat, kept just off the skin, capping the free edge; cure.
Thin layers cure right through; gel on the skin lifts and can cause allergy.
Colour
Two thin coats, cured one at a time.
Thick gel wrinkles, stays soft underneath and can give a heat spike.
Art
Gel paints, liners, foils or gems in gel; cure each layer (a short 'flash' cure holds fine detail if the maker allows).
The design does not move until it is cured.
Top coat
Cover all the art and cap the free edge; cure.
Seals and protects.
Sticky layer
Wipe off the sticky **inhibition layer** with gel cleanser on a lint-free wipe (a no-wipe top coat leaves none).
Air stops the very top of the gel curing, leaving it sticky.
Finish
Cuticle oil on the skin around the nails.
Moisturises after the cleanser.

ul: Use the lamp type (LED or UV) and the time **the gel maker gives**. LED lamps often cure in about 30 to 60 seconds and UV lamps in about 2 minutes, but times vary: never guess.
The hand lies flat, fingers in the centre of the lamp. Cure thumbs on their own so they lie flat too.
If gel touches the skin, clean it off with a brush or orange stick before you cure it.
A **heat spike** (a sudden burning feeling) comes from thick layers or a very strong lamp. Take the hand out, let it cool, then finish the cure.
Gel that is not cured long enough stays soft underneath, wrinkles, lifts and is more likely to cause an allergy.
Light from a window or the lamp cures gel in open bottles and brushes. Keep bottles closed and brushes capped.

blocks.note: Repeated contact with uncured gel can cause an **allergy to acrylates** (red, itchy, swollen skin around the nails, sometimes on the face). Once a person is allergic it usually lasts for life, so she can no longer have gel or acrylic nails, and may react to some dental and medical products. Wear gloves, keep gel off your skin and hers, and cure gel-soaked wipes under the lamp before you bin them.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Apply the top coat over the whole nail and all the art, and cap the free edge. Over raised art and gems, float a full bead of top coat on rather than dragging the brush. Then check every nail in good light and show the client.

ul: The base colour is smooth and even, with no streaks, bubbles or thin patches.
Lines are straight and clean, dots are even, and the design matches the plan.
Both hands balance, and the accent nails match.
There is no product on the cuticles, side walls or skin.
Gems, foils and decals are secure and flat, with no sharp edges.
The top coat covers everything and caps the free edge.

blocks.note: Clean polish off the skin with a fine flat or angled brush dipped in remover and blotted on a towel, run along the cuticle line. Do it before the polish sets. Never scrape it off with a metal tool.
blocks.label: Tip

head: What is on the nail
How to remove it
rows: Ordinary polish and nail art
Hold a remover-soaked pad on the nail for about 10 seconds, then wipe from base to tip
Glitter, foil or gems: wrap the remover pads on the nails in foil for a few minutes, then wipe; ease gems off with an orange stick
Gel polish and gel art
Lightly file the shiny top coat to break the seal; do not file into the nail
Put cotton soaked in acetone remover on each nail and wrap it in foil (or use clips) for the time the maker gives, often about 10 to 15 minutes
Push the softened gel gently from the base to the tip with an orange stick; wrap again if it does not come away
Never force, scrape or peel it
Wash the hands; finish with cuticle oil and hand cream

blocks.note: Never peel gel off. Peeling pulls away the top layers of the nail plate with the gel, leaving thin, weak, white patches that take months to grow out.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Advice
Why
rows: Wear gloves for housework, washing up and gardening
Water and cleaning products soften polish, lift art and dry the skin.
Do not use your nails as tools (opening cans, scraping labels)
This chips the art and breaks the nail.
With ordinary polish, add a thin top coat every two or three days
It keeps the art sealed and shiny.
Use cuticle oil every day
It keeps the cuticles soft and the nails flexible, and prevents hangnails.
Do not pick or peel; come back if a gem loosens or gel lifts
Picking pulls off layers of nail; lifted gel traps water and germs.
Have gel removed at the salon, usually after about 2 to 3 weeks
Safe soak-off protects the nail plate.
Rinse off sea water and pool water; protect the hands in strong sun
Salt, chlorine and sun dry the skin and fade colours.
Report any itching, redness or swelling around the nails
It may be an allergy; she may need a doctor.

ul: Suggest products that help, such as cuticle oil, hand cream, a top coat or a gentle remover. Explain honestly what each does, give the price in J$, and let her decide.
Suggest a date to come back, for removal or a new design.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date, client's name and contact details
07/11/2026, Odette Palmer, Old Harbour
Nail and skin check
Squoval, short to medium; two white spots; no contraindications seen
Allergies
None known
Occasion and design
Office party: nude base, gold striping-tape lines, small gems on ring-finger accent nails
Products and colours
Gel base, two coats nude gel, gel top coat; LED lamp, cured as the maker says
Time and price
75 minutes; J$ 4,500 (agreed before starting)
Aftercare given
Gloves for housework; cuticle oil daily; soak-off at the salon in about 3 weeks
Reactions or problems
None
Signatures
Client; technician (trainee), checked by the instructor

blocks.note: Record cards hold personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act they must be kept private and secure. Before you photograph a client's nails for your portfolio or the salon's page, ask her permission and photograph her hands only; never post her face or name without her written consent.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Cap every bottle and wipe the necks
Clean brushes in the right cleaner and store them covered
Clean the stamping plate and stamper
Bin single-use items; solvent waste in the metal bin
Clean and disinfect metal tools
Wipe the station and lamp with disinfectant
Towels in the laundry bin
Wash your hands

ul: I can name the hazards at the nail station and say how to control fumes, fire, allergy, dust and eye splashes.
I can store nail products safely and put solvent-soaked waste in a lidded metal bin.
I can give first aid for a splash in the eye, fumes, a small cut and a heat spike.
I can clean and disinfect metal tools, treat single-use items correctly, and clean each brush with the right cleaner.
I can name the parts of the nail and the main nail shapes.
I can hold a consultation and explain why I ask about the occasion, her job, allergies, time and price.
I can tell which nail conditions stop the service, which restrict it and which are harmless, and refer a client kindly.
I can use the colour wheel to choose complementary, analogous and monochromatic schemes.
I can plan a balanced design with an accent nail that suits the nail length and the client.
I can prepare natural nails and apply base coat and colour smoothly, capping the free edge.
I can name the main tools and products and say what each is for.
I can make dots, stripes, an ombre, a French tip, marbling and a stamped design, and fix common faults.
I can apply gems, sticker and water-slide decals and transfer foil so that they last.
I can apply, cure and finish gel nail art, wiping off the inhibition layer and keeping gel off the skin.
I can check the quality of my work, remove polish and gel safely, give aftercare advice and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I cap the free edge with top coat, so that the tip is sealed and the art does not chip.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The hard layers of keratin that make up the visible nail.
The part of the nail that grows past the end of the finger.
The hidden part at the base of the nail where new nail cells are made.
The pale half-moon at the base of the nail.
Dead skin stuck to the nail plate at its base.
The living fold of skin at the base of the nail; it must not be cut.
The skin at each side of the nail plate.
A nail shape with a straight edge and softly rounded corners.
A nail shape whose sides taper to a soft, rounded point.
Something that stops a service or means it must be changed.
A fungal infection of the nail.
A bacterial infection of the skin around the nail.
The nail plate lifting away from the nail bed.
White spots on the nail; harmless.
Orange, green and purple, each made from two primaries.
Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel.
Colours next to each other on the colour wheel.
Using tints and shades of one colour.
One nail decorated differently to catch the eye.
Both hands look like a matching pair.
Removes oil and moisture from the nail plate before the base coat.
Protects the nail and helps the colour stick.
Seals and protects the design and adds shine.
Running the brush along the free edge to seal the tip.
A long, thin brush for long, fine lines.
A ball-ended tool for making neat dots.
A fan-shaped brush for streaks and feathered effects.
Colours that blend from one to another, often sponged on.
The curved edge of the tip in a French manicure.
Swirling colours together to look like marble.
Transferring an etched design from a plate to the nail with a stamper.
Thin adhesive tape for straight lines.
A design that is soaked, slid onto the nail and sealed.
A thin metallic film pressed onto tacky foil adhesive.
Polish that hardens only when cured under an LED or UV lamp.
Hardening gel under an LED or UV lamp.
The sticky layer left on some gels after curing.
A sudden burning feeling while gel cures, usually from thick layers.
The strong solvent in many removers and in gel soak-off.
The maker's sheet on a product's hazards, safe use, storage and first aid.
A metal bin with a lid for solvent-soaked waste.
Used on one client only, then thrown away.
The client's record of nail checks, design, products, price, advice and any reactions.

c1.title: Champs colours in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Shanoya Grant, 19, wants her nails in her old school's colours, royal blue and orange, for Champs at the National Stadium next week. She works at a supermarket checkout, handling cash, bags and the scanner all day. Her nails are short and squoval. She asks trainee Renée for rhinestones on all ten nails, and says the art must still look good on the last day of Champs, seven days away.

c2.title: An anniversary dinner in Linstead
c2.text: Mrs. Hyacinth Gayle, 63, a retired teacher, has booked nail art (soft pink with small white flowers) for her 40th wedding anniversary dinner. Trainee Kayon finds that the left middle nail has lifted away from the nail bed at the tip since Mrs. Gayle caught it in a car door last month; the area underneath looks white, with no pain or colour change. Two other nails have small white spots. The skin beside the right ring nail is red, swollen, hot and throbbing, with a yellow bead of pus.

c3.title: Practice tips in the training salon in Spanish Town
c3.text: Trainees at the Centre in Spanish Town are making practice tips for their themed board. Jodian's stamped flowers come out with gaps and missing petals: she scrapes the plate slowly, then wipes her scraper before she picks up the design. Rojae cleaned his gel brush with acetone yesterday and left it uncapped on the window sill; today its bristles are stiff and hard. Kerece has been painting palm leaves with water-based nail art paint.

c4.title: Gel art for a family reunion in Portmore
c4.text: Tashieka Morrison, 33, booked gel colour with gold foil for a family reunion. To save time, trainee Sasha applies the gel colour in one thick coat. While her hand is in the LED lamp, Tashieka snatches it out, saying it burns. After the top coat is cured, the nails feel sticky. Three weeks later Tashieka comes back: the gel is lifting, she has peeled it off two nails at home, and those two nails are thin, with white, rough patches.

c5.title: A hot afternoon in Mandeville
c5.text: It is a hot afternoon at a beauty salon in Mandeville. The air conditioning is off and the windows are shut because of the rain. At trainee Ackeem's station, a pot of acetone has been left open beside the wax heater, and cotton pads soaked in remover are piled in an open plastic tray. Halfway through her nail art, his client, Dahlia, says she has a headache and feels dizzy.

questions.q: Why will royal blue and orange stand out so strongly on Shanoya's nails?
o: They are both primary colours, the brightest on the wheel
They sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
They sit next to each other on the colour wheel
They are both warm colours, so they glow in sunlight
questions.why: Blue and orange are complementary: opposite each other on the colour wheel, they give the strongest contrast. Orange is a secondary colour (red + yellow), and blue is a cool colour, not a warm one.

questions.q: What is the best way to handle Shanoya's wish for rhinestones?
o: Large gems on every nail, so they can be seen from the stands
Gems close to the free edge, where they catch the light
3D charms instead, as they snag less than flat gems
Small, flat gems on the accent nails only, sealed well
questions.why: Her short nails and her job at the checkout mean gems will catch and lift. A few small, flat gems kept to the accent nails, set and sealed well, suit both the design and her daily life; the free edge is where gems catch most.

questions.q: Which choice gives Shanoya the best chance of art that lasts the full week?
o: Gel polish, cured as the maker says, with free edges capped
Ordinary polish in thick coats, so the colour is harder
Ordinary polish with quick-dry drops, which set it hard for good
Gel polish cured for half the time, so it stays flexible
questions.why: Gel cured correctly lasts about 2 to 3 weeks, and capping seals the tips. Thick polish stays soft and dents, quick-dry only dries the surface, and under-cured gel stays soft, lifts and raises the risk of allergy.

questions.q: Shanoya asks for a design that makes her short nails look longer. What should Renée suggest?
o: Wide horizontal bands of blue and orange across each nail
A deep white French tip on all ten of her nails
Fine vertical stripes running from the cuticle to the tip
Dark blue polish painted over the side walls as well
questions.why: Vertical lines lead the eye along the nail and make it look longer and slimmer. Horizontal bands and a deep tip cut the nail into short sections, and polish on the side walls looks messy and lifts.

questions.q: Which of Mrs. Gayle's nails can Kayon prepare and paint as normal?
o: The nail that has lifted, if it is kept short
The nails with the small white spots
The right ring nail, if Kayon wears gloves
All ten nails, once the pus has been wiped
questions.why: White spots (leuconychia) usually come from small knocks and are not a contraindication. The lifted nail needs a restricted service, and the red, swollen, pus-filled finger is an infection that must not be worked on.

questions.q: How should Kayon treat the left middle nail that has lifted from the nail bed?
o: Keep it short with a light design, and never push anything under it
Clean under the lifted part with a fine file, then hide it under gems
Run nail glue under the lifted part to stick it back down
Press the lifted edge down firmly before the base coat goes on
questions.why: Onycholysis restricts the service. Tools or glue under the plate can injure the nail bed and trap germs, so keep it short and light, and suggest a doctor if it does not improve or changes colour.

questions.q: What should Kayon do about the red, swollen, throbbing skin by the right ring nail?
o: Trim the swollen skin away with clean nippers, then carry on
Tell her it is a fungal infection and sell her a cream for it
Paint around it carefully and mention it on the record card
Tell her privately it needs checking, and suggest a doctor
questions.why: Red, hot, painful skin with pus is likely a bacterial infection around the nail. Do not work on it or name a disease; explain kindly and privately, refer her to a doctor, and record what you saw.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason Jodian's stamped flowers have gaps?
o: Her stamper is new, so its head is still too soft
She held the scraper at an angle to the plate
The polish dried on the plate before she picked it up
Her base colour was much too dark for the printed flowers to show
questions.why: Stamping polish dries on the plate within seconds, so the scrape and the pick-up must follow each other at once. Holding the scraper at an angle (about 45°) is correct, and gaps are not caused by the base colour.

questions.q: Why did Rojae's gel brush go stiff and hard?
o: Daylight on the sill cured the gel left in the bristles
The acetone reacted with the gel and set it like glue
He did not rinse the bristles with clean water first
Gel always hardens in the air overnight, even in a dark room
questions.why: Gel cures when light reaches it, and daylight through a window is enough. Gel brushes are wiped, cleaned with the maker's gel cleanser, capped and stored away from light.

questions.q: How should Kerece clean the brush she used for the water-based palm leaves?
o: Soak it in acetone for several minutes, then leave it to dry in the sun
Rinse it in clean water while the paint is still wet, then wipe it
Wipe it on a dry towel and let the paint dry in the bristles
Dip it in gel cleanser and store it uncapped on the trolley
questions.why: Water-based nail art paint comes out with water while it is wet. Harsh solvents and dried paint spoil the bristles, so clean it straight away, reshape it and store it covered.

questions.q: What most likely caused the burning feeling when Tashieka's hand was in the lamp?
o: An allergy to the light given out by the LED lamp
Too short a curing time for the colour coat
A heat spike from gel applied in a thick coat
The gold foil heating up while it was in the lamp
questions.why: Thick gel gives off a lot of heat as it cures, which the client feels as a sudden burn (a heat spike). Thin coats, each cured as the maker says, prevent it; she should take her hand out and let it cool.

questions.q: What should Sasha do about the sticky surface after curing the top coat?
o: Cure it again and again until the stickiness goes
Wipe it off with gel cleanser on a lint-free wipe
Leave it on, as it protects the art for a day
Buff it away with a coarse file before she leaves
questions.why: Many gels leave a sticky inhibition layer, where air stopped the very top from curing. It is wiped off with the maker's cleanser; more curing will not remove it, and buffing would scratch the finish.

questions.q: How should Sasha remove the gel that is left on Tashieka's other nails?
o: Peel it away gently, since it is already lifting
Buff it all off with a coarse file to save time
Soak her fingers in warm, soapy water until the gel floats away
File off the shine, soak it in acetone wraps, then ease it off
questions.why: Breaking the top coat lets the acetone reach the gel; once it softens, it is pushed off gently with an orange stick. Peeling and heavy filing take layers of nail with them, and soapy water does not dissolve gel.

questions.q: Why are the two nails Tashieka peeled now thin with white, rough patches?
o: Layers of the nail plate came away with the gel
The gel colour has stained the nail plate white
Acetone in the gel dried the nails from inside
The lamp light bleached the nail under the gel
questions.why: Gel bonds to the top layers of the nail plate, so peeling it tears those layers off. The damage grows out slowly, over months; she needs cuticle oil, gentle care and salon removal from now on.

questions.q: Dahlia says she has a headache and feels dizzy. What should Ackeem do first?
o: Give her a painkiller and finish the last nails quickly
Spray air freshener to cover the smell of the fumes
Stop, and take her into fresh air to sit down
Turn on the lamp's fan and carry on more slowly
questions.why: Fumes in a closed room can cause headaches and dizziness. Stop work, get her into fresh air and let her sit, then close the bottles and ventilate; get medical help if she does not recover. Air freshener only adds more vapour.

questions.q: Which item at Ackeem's station is the greatest fire risk?
o: The bottles of base coat with their lids screwed on
The open pot of acetone beside the wax heater
The LED lamp, which is plugged in but switched off
The clean towels folded on the lower trolley shelf
questions.why: Acetone is very flammable and gives off vapour that can catch fire from a heat source. Solvents must be kept closed, in small amounts, away from heaters, flames and sparks.

questions.q: Which change would do most to cut the fumes at Ackeem's station?
o: Pour the remover into a wide bowl so it lasts longer
Use bigger cotton pads so less remover drips off
Open the windows or run extraction, and cap the bottles
Turn the lamp to a hotter setting so polish dries faster
questions.why: Fumes are controlled by fresh air or extraction and by keeping bottles closed. Solvent-soaked pads also belong in a lidded metal bin, not an open tray, and an open bowl only lets more vapour escape.

questions.q: Months after trapping her finger in a door, a client has a dent that has grown halfway up her nail. Which part of the nail was most likely injured?
o: The free edge, which grows past the fingertip
The hyponychium, the skin under the free edge
The side walls that hold the nail plate in place
The matrix, where new nail cells are formed
questions.why: The matrix makes the nail, so an injury there shows as a dent or ridge in the new nail, which then grows out slowly (about 3 mm a month). Do not dig at the base of the nail when you prepare it.

questions.q: A client with slim fingers and strong nails wants a shape whose sides taper to a soft, rounded point. Which shape is this?
o: Squoval
Square
Almond
Round
questions.why: An almond nail tapers from both sides to a soft point. Square and squoval have a straight free edge, and round simply follows the fingertip with little length.

questions.q: When you paint French tips on all ten nails, what makes the set look professional?
o: Smile lines of the same depth and curve on every nail
A deeper white tip on the thumbs than on the fingers
A straight smile line on each nail, whatever its shape
A white tip that reaches halfway down the nail bed
questions.why: The smile line follows the natural curve of the free edge and is matched in depth on every nail and on both hands. Uneven, straight or very deep tips look careless and unbalanced.
